verdict.reasoning: Patient states main problem is left arm numbness and tingling for at least two weeks: "I can't quite move my left arm... it's numb... tingling in my fingertips" and "it's probably been, I'd say for at least two weeks and it's kind of gotten worse."

She links onset to starting boxing: "I've started taking this boxing class... I've been taking boxing class for a few weeks and I feel like maybe it's probably been, I'd say for at least two weeks" referring to numbness/tingling.

She reports symptoms persisted/worsened despite massage and hot baths: "because it hasn't gotten better, I tried to get a massage. It's not better. Or you know, try to take warm baths. It's not better."

She describes mild weakness and piano difficulty: "I play a little bit of a piano and so I just noticed that it's... been kind of harder to get the notes" and agrees to mild weakness when asked: "So you would say there's a mild weakness? Mild, yes."

Distribution described as palmar digits 2–4 from elbow down: "I can feel it both in my... elbow and then in my arm as well as in my hand" and "it's my second, third and fourth finger" and "it's the... front side" (palm).
She reports shoulder discomfort with movement: "sometimes I will feel it in my shoulder. Like if I try to... move like in boxing and stuff, I will even like maybe feel a little bit of... pain."
She clearly denies neck pain: Doctor: "Any neck pain at all?" Patient: "No, not. No neck pain."

She describes a bad cold/flu about a month ago lasting around two weeks: "I also had a really bad cold like a month ago... I was sick for probably good, like, two weeks... I think I must have had some kind of like a flu or something."
Regarding general health: "But in general, I'm pretty healthy... I don't really have any medical problems."
She uses ibuprofen as needed: "I do take ibuprofen just because my, my muscles were sore a little bit... So I've just kind of taken ibuprofen for that."
She states regular vitamin D use: "vitamin D, I take."
She takes iron inconsistently: "my GP really wants me to take iron supplements, but you know, there are this like huge pill, so I, most of the time I just forget."
She uses melatonin as needed: "And then sometimes I take melatonin to help me sleep."
Father's history: "I know that my dad has... I think it's hypothyroidism" and "he's got some autoimmune stuff going on."
Mother's diabetes: "my mom, she's... got diabetes, type 2."
Mother's hypertension: "she's got hypertension."
Mother's high cholesterol: "she's got... high cholesterol."
She started boxing and works out regularly: "I've started taking this boxing class" and "I work out a lot."

She describes a heavy drinking episode at a party: "we kind of went crazy and we were like out partying until, you know, late hours, and I just got uncharacteristically drunk for me." This supports occasional heavy alcohol use.
She indicates right-hand dominance: "I can grasp a glass. But because I use my right hand most of the time, you know, I'm not left handed."

Left upper limb paresthesia and mild weakness are supported, but the transcript only mentions MS as a possible diagnosis and suggests "more than just the box[ing]"; it does not list a differential including peripheral neuropathy, cervical radiculopathy, or overuse.

Transient left visual loss and concern for MS/demyelinating disease are supported, but the note’s phrasing "optic neuritis" and explicit need to rule out demyelinating disease are not stated; the doctor only says "Sometimes... multiple sclerosis... people... can have visual problems like what you've experienced."
A recent viral illness is described, but the clinician never states it is considered a precipitating factor; that causal interpretation is new.
Jaw and knuckle pain are mentioned, but the clinician does not explicitly assess them as "mild musculoskeletal pain"; that characterization is inferred and not stated.

An urgent neurology referral is planned: "I'm going to do an urgent, very urgent neurology referral... What that might entail is the brain scan and things like that." However, there is no mention of MRI of the spine or a "full neurological work-up"; specifying spine MRI and full work-up adds unsupported details.

He provides red-flag education: "if there's any weakness... progresses to your legs or there's any kind of headaches, vomiting, fits, and your visual symptoms are getting worse and not getting better, then that would be an A" (emergency). This covers increased weakness, leg involvement, visual loss, headache, vomiting, and seizures/fits.

The doctor says, "No, that's something we can't do... first we need to... firm diagnosis," when asked about drugs, but does not advise continuing ibuprofen or explicitly state "start no new medications until neurology review." Those management instructions are not given.
There is no advice in the transcript about remaining active or avoiding boxing drills; this counseling is not discussed.
No explicit follow-up plan is stated such as "follow up after neurology assessment or sooner if symptoms progress." Only referral and ED red-flag advice are given.

She describes transient left peripheral vision loss: "I all of a sudden just couldn't see from... my left eye. Like, I lost some... field of vision" and duration: "maybe like 20 minutes or so" and that it was a few weeks ago.
She reports fatigue episodes: "sometimes I'll get kind of tired" and "this morning, for example, I just felt really fatigued and I couldn't even get myself to the gym."
She notes "tired" headaches: "Sometimes I get headaches, but I think they're just tired headaches."
She denies seizures/fits: Doctor: "you've not had experienced anything like a seizure fit, anything like that?" Patient: "Oh, no, no, no, no. Nothing like that."

Seizure explanation includes loss of consciousness and she denies this: Doctor: "Like when you lose consciousness and you start shaking?" Patient: "Oh, no, no, no, no. Nothing like that." This implies denial of loss of consciousness events.
She reports normal gait: Doctor: "your weakness is only in your left arm, leg, walking and all this. Normal?" Patient: "Walking is normal. Yeah."
